title: AgroSense ARIA
lede: My M.Tech final-year project: an AI farming platform that keeps working without the internet. ESP32-S3 sensor nodes on my own 4-layer board form a self-healing LoRa mesh and report to a Raspberry Pi that runs seven ML models and a three-tier voice assistant.

meta.Stack: ESP32-S3 · LoRa · Raspberry Pi · Edge AI

hero.alt: The ARIA dashboard running on the Raspberry Pi hub
hero.caption: ARIA dashboard, live

p: ARIA is my M.Tech final-year project. It's an AI farming platform that keeps working with no internet connection. A mesh of ESP32-S3 sensor nodes talks over LoRa to a Raspberry Pi hub, and everything happens on hardware out in the field: the sensing, the predictions, the irrigation decisions and the assistant the farmer talks to.
The nodes run on the AgroSense boards I designed alongside it. Revision 3 is the hardware in use now.

Each node is a root hub, a sub-hub or a leaf, and the network works with anywhere from 2 to 100 of them. When the network needs it, a leaf can be promoted to a sub-hub, so losing one node doesn't cut the network in half.

I split the airtime with TDMA so a hundred nodes on one frequency don't talk over each other, and an RTC-based time sync keeps everyone's slots lined up. I wrote about 7,260 lines of ESP32-S3 firmware for this, with AES-128 on the link. The nodes deep-sleep between readings, and that's what stretches the battery life out to years.

The Raspberry Pi runs seven models, all offline: disease detection, irrigation scheduling, fertiliser planning, yield prediction, crop recommendation, anomaly detection on the sensor data, and an ensemble that combines them into one plan.

The assistant the farmer uses is a three-tier cascade. It uses the cloud when there's signal and a local model when there isn't, and you can speak to it and hear it answer in English, Hindi or Telugu.

I put the irrigation automation behind a four-level autonomy controller, which goes from just giving advice up to acting on its own. Every action is logged, and anything it does automatically can be undone for 60 seconds. I did that because watering mistakes cost money and take a long time to fix.

specs: Claude Haiku 4.5 → Claude Code CLI → Ollama qwen2.5:0.5b
Vosk STT, Edge-TTS — EN / HI / TE

metrics.s: all inference runs on the farm

title: AgroSense Node rev 3
lede: The current version of my AgroSense node: four copper layers, solar MPPT charging with a selectable panel input, a matched LoRa front end, and three supply rails I can switch on and off separately.

hero.alt: 3D render of the AgroSense revision 3 board, top side
hero.caption: Revision 3 — top side

p: I built the AgroSense node in three revisions. Rev 1 was a 2-layer prototype, rev 2 moved to four layers, and rev 3 is the one out in the field. Each time, I fixed what the last board's bring-up had shown me in the next layout instead of patching it on the bench.
Rev 3 is a four-layer mixed-signal board, and it's the hardware ARIA runs on.

It has a LoRa radio with a matched RF feed and a U.FL connector, so the antenna can be picked for each site without redesigning the board. I kept the antenna keepout and the stitched ground around the feed well away from the switching and digital parts. Having that solid ground plane under the radio is the main reason I went to four layers.

For power there's solar MPPT charging with a jumper to select the panel voltage, Li-ion charging and protection, and a USB-C input. The 3.3 V, 5 V and 12 V rails can each be turned on separately, so sensors that aren't in use get switched off between readings instead of sitting powered.

Rev 3 added microSD logging, an IMU, I²S audio, RGB status lights, a smaller outline, and I²C and GPIO headers for adding things in the field. Before each run I did a DRC and DFM review and then sent out the Gerbers, BOM and netlists.
You can see all four copper layers and both 3D renders in the gallery below.

specs: LoRa SX1262, matched feed to U.FL

title: AgroSense Node rev 2
lede: The revision where I moved to four copper layers: MPPT solar charging and a multi-rail power tree on an 82 × 80 mm board, and the bring-up that showed me two real layout mistakes.

hero.alt: AgroSense 2.0 four-layer board, 3D render of the top side
hero.caption: AgroSense 2.0 — top side

p: I built the AgroSense node in three revisions. Rev 1 was a 2-layer prototype, rev 2 moved to four layers, and rev 3 is the one out in the field. Each time, I fixed what the last board's bring-up had shown me in the next layout instead of patching it on the bench.
Rev 2 is where I went to four copper layers. It's 82 × 80 mm with 195 components.

Solar comes in through an MPPT charge controller with a wide input range, so the same board works with panels of quite different sizes. I kept battery charging and reverse-current protection separate from the harvesting stage, with a load switch between the battery and everything after it.

A buck converter makes the 3.3 V logic rail, and boost converters make 5 V and a selectable 9 or 12 V for sensors that need more. Keeping them separate instead of sharing one supply is what lets me shut most of the board down between readings.
The first assembled boards had two faults. Both were my mistakes, and both were in the layout, not in the parts I chose.

I had routed the USB data pair to the UART bridge the wrong way round, so the board wouldn't show up on a computer. And the boost converter didn't route cleanly: the ground return and the vias around the switching node weren't good enough.
I fixed both in rev 3 instead of patching them on the bench. The board did work, but those two mistakes taught me more than the parts that worked first time.

title: AgroSense Node rev 1
lede: The two-layer prototype that started AgroSense. It sampled soil and weather on a schedule, slept between readings using an RTC, charged from solar, and sent its data over a long-range link to a gateway.

hero.alt: AgroSense 1.0 node block diagram showing sensing, power and radio sections
hero.caption: System block diagram

p: I built the AgroSense node in three revisions. Rev 1 was a 2-layer prototype, rev 2 moved to four layers, and rev 3 is the one out in the field. Each time, I fixed what the last board's bring-up had shown me in the next layout instead of patching it on the bench.
Rev 1 is the two-layer prototype. Its job was to prove the idea worked before I spent money on four layers.

It measured soil moisture, water level, temperature and humidity at set times and sent the readings to a gateway, so nobody had to walk the field with a meter. The controller, radio, real-time clock, solar charging and the wired sensor connections were all on one board.

I designed it to be asleep most of the time. An RTC wakes the controller on schedule, and the board goes back into deep sleep between readings. That's what lets a node last a whole season instead of needing a visit every two weeks.
The two-layer layout worked, but it didn't leave me room to give the radio a better ground plane, and the power section was more cramped than I wanted. Both of those went straight into rev 2.

title: Dletabotix Kit Hardware
lede: Two boards for a classroom robotics kit: a multi-function controller that students put together themselves, and a USB-host programmer that reflashes a whole bench of BBC micro:bits without a PC.

hero.alt: Dletabotix kit hardware — artwork not published
hero.caption: Artwork not published

p: At Dletabotix I design the electronics for the company's classroom robotics kits. So far that's two boards, both low-cost 2-layer designs, because schools buy them by the dozen.

What shapes both boards is that students will plug things in wrong, and that's part of how they learn. So every external connector is keyed so a sensor can't go in backwards, students solder the through-hole parts themselves, and the microcontroller sits in a socket. If a wiring mistake kills it, you swap the chip instead of reworking the board.

It's an Arduino Nano carrier with dual H-bridge drivers for four motors, keyed connectors for ultrasonic, IR, light and RGB modules, and Bluetooth so it can be driven from a phone. Power comes from a protected two-cell Li-ion charger fed by USB-C or a barrel jack, with switching regulators for the rails. I kept the charging current and the load current separate, so a robot on the bench with a cable plugged in can still drive.
Normally you program a micro:bit by dragging a file onto the USB drive it shows up as. That's fine for one board, but painful when one teacher has thirty.

This board uses an ESP32-S3 in USB host mode to mount that drive itself and copy the firmware onto it, either over Wi-Fi or from on-board storage. You load the file once and then plug in each micro:bit in turn. A TFT screen and buttons guide you through it, and the micro:bit only gets 5 V when the firmware switches it on.

For each board I do the first-article checks (power rails, peripherals and current draw), and then I track down faults at the signal level with a scope and a logic analyser across the prototype versions.

I also wrote the kit's mode handling in firmware. The line sensors calibrate themselves every time they run instead of relying on a trimmer set at the factory, so the kit works on whatever floor the classroom has.

specs: Microcontroller module on a carrier socket
Keyed connectors — ultrasonic, IR, light, RGB
BBC micro:bit, via its USB mass-storage interface
Firmware-enabled 5 V to the connected board
Over Wi-Fi or from on-board storage

title: Grid OS Telematics & Audio
lede: The boards inside Grid OS's vehicle trackers and cellular audio devices. I designed 2- and 4-layer boards in Altium, and the production panels they ship on.

hero.alt: Close-up of a densely populated radio front end — shielded IC, crystals and matching network
hero.caption: Radio front end

p: At Grid OS I worked on the boards inside their vehicle trackers and their cellular audio devices, the countertop and handheld units that read payments out loud.

Both are built around a cellular module with a SIM interface, battery-backed power, and an antenna that has to work inside someone else's enclosure. I did the schematics and layout on 2- and 4-layer stackups in Altium: impedance-controlled routing for the USB and radio lines, antenna keepouts and ground fencing, the audio codec section, and the switching supplies that power everything.

I also drew the production panels the boards ship on, with V-score separation, breakaway rails, fiducials and tooling holes, laid out for the assembler's machines and not just to fit. Three of them are in the gallery below.

Each design went out as a complete manufacturing package, not just a board file: Gerbers, drill files, a test-point map, an impedance profile and a BOM, after design-rule and manufacturability checks.

specs: Antenna keepouts, ground fencing, impedance control
Panelisation, Gerbers, drill, test points, BOM

title: 32-bit ALU — RTL to GDSII
lede: A 32-bit ALU I took through a full open-source chip design flow: 29 operations, a Brent–Kung adder, 7,372 standard cells placed and 8,135 nets routed with zero DRC violations on 0.18 µm.

meta.Programme: NIELIT Centre of Excellence in Chip Design

hero.alt: Detail of the ALU standard-cell layout in Magic, showing routed metal over cell rows
hero.caption: Magic layout detail

p: During my internship at NIELIT's Centre of Excellence in Chip Design, I took a 32-bit ALU all the way from Verilog to a GDSII file ready for fabrication, using only open-source tools: Yosys, GrayWolf, Qrouter and Magic.
It does 29 operations: signed and unsigned add, subtract, multiply and divide, all sixteen boolean functions, and three kinds of shift.

For fast addition I used a Brent–Kung parallel prefix adder. It needs more wiring, but the carry path grows logarithmically instead of linearly. Even so, it ended up being the critical path of the whole design.

I made multiply and divide sequential state machines that take 32 cycles, instead of building them as combinational arrays. That was on purpose: a full 32-bit combinational multiplier would have taken most of the cells, for operations that don't need to be that fast here.
The result was 7,372 standard cells, a 5.24 ns critical path (about 190 MHz), and 8,135 nets routed with zero DRC violations on 0.18 µm. It passed all 66 randomised tests across three seeds.
For me it showed that the open-source flow is good enough for real digital blocks, not just classroom examples.

title: Arduino Nano — 12 V Input
lede: An Arduino Nano I redesigned for 12 V supplies. It keeps the same pinout, but takes 12 V through a switching regulator, uses USB-C with ESD protection on the data lines, and brings out proper debug headers.

hero.alt: 3D render of the custom Arduino Nano board, top side
hero.caption: 3D render, top

p: A normal Arduino Nano uses a linear regulator on its input. If you feed it 12 V, which is what industrial and car supplies give you, the regulator turns the extra voltage into heat, and that limits how much the rest of the board can draw before it shuts down.
I kept the Nano pinout so existing shields and code still work, and redesigned the power input.
A buck converter brings 12 V down to 5 V, and an LDO makes 3.3 V from that, so the analogue rail doesn't get the switching ripple directly.

I swapped mini-B for USB-C and put ESD protection on the data lines, because that's what usually kills development boards on a busy bench. On top of the normal headers I added separate UART, I²C and ICSP headers. That sounds small, but it really helps when you're trying to clip a logic analyser onto a bus that's hidden under a shield.

specs: Nano pinout, plus UART, I²C and ICSP

title: Network Rover + Surveillance
lede: My B.Tech final-year project: a Wi-Fi rover with live video, a pan-tilt camera and a robotic arm, plus cloud telemetry and an eight-channel relay board for home automation. It pulled together everything I'd learned in four years.

hero.alt: Network controlled rover with robotic arm and camera mast
hero.caption: Completed rover

p: This was my B.Tech final-year project, and it's really three things in one build: a rover you can drive with live video, a robotic arm you can control remotely, and a home automation controller. You reach all of them over the network from one interface.

A Raspberry Pi runs the Python side: camera streaming, talking to the cloud and parsing commands. Arduino boards handle the real-time jobs like motors, servo timing and reading sensors. Splitting it that way is what stops the video from stuttering every time a motor changes direction.

The camera sits on a two-axis mount driven through an I²C servo controller, which takes sixteen servo channels off the Pi's GPIO. Ultrasonic and IR sensors handle obstacles, and fire and temperature sensors cover the surveillance side.
Telemetry goes to a cloud service for logging and remote commands, and you can switch appliances through Google Assistant as well as from the dashboard.

Power comes from a Li-ion pack with a BMS, feeding a step-down converter. The rover runs motors, servos, a Pi and a camera at the same time, and when the motors start and the supply dips, the Pi is the first thing to brown out.

specs: Li-ion pack with BMS, XL4015E step-down

title: Night Vision Rover
lede: A Raspberry Pi rover I drove over the network from a Python program, with an infrared camera on a pan-tilt servo mount so it can see in the dark.

hero.alt: Night vision rover chassis with infrared camera mounted on servos
hero.caption: Rover with camera mast

p: It's a Raspberry Pi rover that I drove over the network from a Python program on my PC. Driving, the camera angle and the lights all go over the same link. The infrared camera is the main point: it works in the dark.
The camera is aimed by two servos, one horizontal and one vertical, controlled through an I²C servo driver so the Pi doesn't have to generate servo pulses itself while it's streaming video.
Commands come in over Wi-Fi, get parsed, and go to separate modules for driving, lights and camera angle. Keeping those separate instead of in one big loop made it easy to keep adding to.
I reused both the camera mount and the way I parsed commands in my final-year rover.

title: Bluetooth Multi-Task Rover
lede: One rover with three behaviours: manual driving from an Android app, line following and obstacle avoidance, with the current mode and messages shown on an LCD.

hero.alt: Bluetooth multi-task rover on a workbench with LCD and sensor array
hero.caption: Assembled rover

p: The rover takes single-letter commands over Bluetooth from an Android app and switches between three modes: manual driving, following a line with infrared sensors, and avoiding obstacles with an ultrasonic sensor.
A 16×2 LCD shows the current mode, live sensor readings, or any text you send from your phone. That last one turned out to be the feature everyone wanted to play with.
It's Arduino C++ on an Uno, with the motors on a dual H-bridge. I wrote the mode switching as a state machine, so changing modes is clean and a motor doesn't stay stuck on from the previous mode.
Each behaviour is its own function built on shared driving functions, which made it easy to add a vacuum to the same code later for my cleaning robot.

title: Bluetooth Home Automation
lede: Mains appliances switched by relays from an Android app over Bluetooth, with a scene mode that switches several devices with one command.

hero.alt: Bluetooth home automation build with relay modules wired to appliances
hero.caption: Relay control build

p: An Arduino switches lights, fans and other mains appliances through relays, and you control it from an Android app over Bluetooth. Each command maps to a device and an action. I also added a scene mode that switches several devices with one command, so you can shut a room down without sending five separate commands.

Because it switches mains voltage, I was careful with it. The relay modules are opto-isolated from the logic side, the low-voltage and mains parts are kept physically apart, and it runs from a proper regulated supply instead of a bench adapter.
The firmware keeps track of each relay's state instead of guessing it, so it always knows what's on.

title: Vacuum Cleaning Robot
lede: A cleaning robot I built on an acrylic chassis I cut myself, with a suction fan, a PWM-controlled sweep brush, ultrasonic collision avoidance, and an infrared sensor that stops it driving off steps.

hero.alt: Autonomous vacuum cleaning robot on a custom acrylic chassis
hero.caption: Completed robot

p: I cut the chassis from acrylic and built the robot on it: two DC motors on an H-bridge, a centrifugal fan for suction, and a sweep brush, with its speed set by PWM, that pushes dirt into the intake. Bluetooth starts and stops it, and a separate switch turns the cleaning parts on, so you can move it around without the fan and brush running.
It avoids walls with an ultrasonic sensor. To stop it driving off a step, there's an infrared sensor pointed at the floor. It's cheap and it works reliably.
It sends its status over serial, which helped more than I expected: watching the sensor values live was the only practical way to tune the thresholds for each floor.

title: Colophon
lede: How I built this site: a 3D portfolio made with Vite and three.js, where the board in the background is my real AgroSense rev 3, rebuilt from its layout data.

p: I wanted the site to look like the work I do. The board floating behind every page is my AgroSense rev 3 node. The model comes from the Blender scene I made for the board's build video, and the copper, solder mask, silkscreen and gold pads are drawn by a shader from images made out of the real Gerbers.

As you scroll, the camera moves between close-ups of real parts on that board: the ESP32-S3 module, the 6-pin header, the SOIC next to the card slot and the USB-C edge. Then it flips over to the bottom side, where the RGB LEDs light up.
It's Vite and three.js, with GSAP ScrollTrigger and Lenis for the scrolling, and no UI framework. The cards, filters and contact form are frosted glass, so the 3D shows through them.
The board model is about 210,000 triangles, compressed with Draco. If WebGL or the model doesn't load, the page still works and reads normally.

I measured the frame rate while I built it. The biggest costs turned out to be CSS, not the 3D: 116 blurred capability chips and a full-page grain overlay. Fixing those two did more than any change to the renderer.
If you have reduced motion turned on, the smooth scrolling, reveals and animation all back off.
An earlier version of this portfolio was adapted from R-TharunReddy/My_Portfolio under its original licence. None of that code is left, but the site ran on it for a long time, so I want to credit it.
Source: github.com/Alita-Tempest/Portfolio.

title: nRF54 Audible Altimeter
lede: A small board I designed around the Seeed XIAO nRF54LM20A for an altimeter that tells you your altitude by sound. All of it had to fit in a 56 × 52 × 11 mm case, along with a speaker and a battery.

hero.alt: 3D render of the nRF54 altimeter board: XIAO nRF54LM20A module, debug header, speaker and battery connectors
hero.caption: 3D view — XIAO nRF54LM20A carrier, top side

p: The client wanted an altimeter that beeps instead of showing a screen, and it had to fit inside a 56 × 52 × 11 mm case. The catch was that the same case also holds a 36 mm speaker and a 31 × 31 mm Li-Po battery, so those two parts decided the layout before I placed anything else. The board ended up at about 38 × 45 mm.

I built it around the XIAO nRF54LM20A module, soldered flat onto the board through its castellated edges. The module already handles the radio, USB-C charging and the 3.3 V supply, so my board only had to add the sensor, the audio and the battery protection.

body.h: How it measures and makes sound
p: Altitude comes from a Bosch BMP581 pressure sensor on I²C. I gave it its own corner of the board, and two routed slots partly separate that corner from the module and the amplifier.

For sound I used a MAX98357A, a small I²S class-D amplifier that drives the speaker through a two-pin JST connector. I wired its shutdown pin to a GPIO so the firmware can switch it off between beeps and save battery. The gain is set with resistors, and I left 0 Ω and 470 pF footprints on the outputs in case EMC testing shows we need a filter there. A 47 µF tantalum capacitor keeps the supply steady when the amplifier pulls current in bursts.
The Li-Po goes through a protection circuit before it reaches the module. I used an FS312F-G with an FS8205A dual MOSFET, which cuts the battery off if it's overcharged, drained too far or shorted.

For programming and debugging I put a single 1.5 mm-pitch six-pin header on the board. It gives SWD access to both the nRF54 and the SAMD11 debug chip on the module, and I labelled the pins on the back. Next to it are 3V3 and GND test points, so I can check the supply during bring-up.

specs: MAX98357A I²S class-D amplifier, JST speaker connector
6-pin SWD header for the nRF54 and the SAMD11
About 38 × 45 mm, 2 copper layers, EasyEDA Pro

title: ESP32 Battery Powered Controller-RevD
lede: Revision D of a battery-powered controller I designed around the ESP32-WROOM-32E. It runs a servo, RGB LEDs and a buzzer, and most of my effort went into making the battery last.

hero.alt: 3D render of the ESP32 Rev D board: ESP32-WROOM-32E module, boost converter, slide switch and push button
hero.caption: 3D view — ESP32-WROOM-32E controller, top side

p: The board runs a servo, a string of addressable RGB LEDs and a buzzer, all from a battery. A tilt switch is the main input. I added a 32.768 kHz crystal so the ESP32 keeps accurate time while it's in deep sleep, and an I²C header with an interrupt line for an external RTC.

It's 53 × 34 mm on two layers, with parts on both sides. I moved the battery fuse, the power-switch MOSFETs, the buzzer and the connectors to the bottom, which left the top free for the ESP32 module and the power circuits.

The power switch is a small slide switch, but it doesn't carry the load current. It only pulls the gate of two P-MOSFETs in parallel, and those connect the fused battery to the rest of the board. From there an ME6211 regulator gives the ESP32 a 3.3 V supply that's always on.

The 5 V comes from an MT3608 boost converter. A boost converter that's only switched off still lets battery voltage through its inductor and diode, so I added a P-MOSFET that disconnects its input completely when 5 V isn't needed. The servo gets its own switched 5 V supply with a 100 µF capacitor next to it. I put a pull-down on every enable line, so nothing turns on by accident while the ESP32 is still starting up.
To read the battery voltage I used a 1 MΩ / 1 MΩ divider, so measuring it only costs about 2 µA.

The ESP32 works at 3.3 V but the LEDs expect a 5 V data signal, so the data line goes through a 74AHCT1G125 buffer powered from 5 V. The buzzer is driven by a MOSFET with a flyback diode. Its footprint overlaps a three-pin servo header, so the board can be built with one or the other, and I wrote a custom DRC rule to allow that overlap.
When it was done I released the Gerbers, drill files, BOM, a JLCPCB pick-and-place file and a STEP model, after running DRC against JLCPCB's rules.

specs: 53 × 34 mm, 2 copper layers, parts on both sides
Fused input, slide switch on the gate of paralleled P-MOSFETs
MT3608 boost with a P-MOSFET input disconnect
Separately switched 5 V rail, 100 µF bulk
Tilt switch, push button, battery-voltage ADC
Gerber, drill, BOM, JLCPCB pick-and-place, STEP
